CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response
Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning

Yafei Zhang    Songshuo Lu    Sicong Liao    Zhi Chen    Yaohua Tang Affiliation: Moore Threads AI
Abstract

Recent years have witnessed the rapid adoption of reinforcement learning (RL) in large language model (LLM) post-training, with substantial gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation. In practical systems, however, policy updates and differences between rollout and training engines can make sampled responses off-policy. Sequence-level masking addresses this mismatch by deciding whether an entire response should contribute to optimization. A common masking rule uses the length-normalized geometric mean of sampled token probability ratios. Its signed log-ratios can cancel across positions, concealing substantial bidirectional policy drift. We propose Cancellation-Aware Response Masking (CARM), a sequence-level mask that takes the absolute value of each token log-ratio before averaging, preventing opposing probability changes from canceling. We prove that accepted responses satisfy a joint bound on the fraction of sampled-token ratios outside a prescribed band and their mean log-distance beyond its boundaries. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that CARM improves mean@16 averaged over AIME 2024/2025/2026 and BeyondAIME by up to 3.133.13 percentage points over geometric-mean masking, and increases average pass@1 across four code benchmarks by 2.882.88 points over the strongest evaluated baseline. These findings support CARM as a theoretically grounded and effective method for response-level off-policy control in LLM reinforcement learning.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely used to improve the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs), building on advances in preference-based alignment and execution-feedback learning (Ouyang et al., 2022; Le et al., 2022). In an ideal on-policy setting, responses are generated by the same policy that is being optimized. In practical systems, however, several effects introduce policy mismatch. Mini-batch optimization makes stored responses stale as the policy changes, while actor–learner latency can delay their use. High-throughput rollout engines may also differ from the training backend in batching, numerical precision, and kernel implementations (Yao et al., 2025; Sheng et al., 2025). Consequently, the policy being updated can assign substantially different probabilities to sampled tokens than the rollout policy that generated them.

Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) regulate policy updates through clipping in their token-level surrogate losses (Schulman et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). Clipping changes how individual tokens contribute to the loss, but does not keep every current-to-rollout probability ratio within a prescribed interval. It also does not decide whether an entire response should participate in the update. Sequence-level masking complements clipping by making this decision from a score that summarizes mismatch across the response. Trust Region Masking (TRM), for example, motivates such filtering through an analysis of how policy mismatch affects optimization over long autoregressive sequences (Li et al., 2026).

A simple response-level criterion is geometric-mean masking: it takes the geometric mean of the token probability ratios and retains responses when this aggregate is close to one. We refer to this baseline as GeoMean. In log space, this aggregation corresponds to averaging signed token log-ratios, as used in DeepSeek-V3.2’s off-policy sequence mask (Liu et al., 2025a). The problem is that positive and negative log-ratios can cancel. For example, token ratios of 1010 and 0.10.1 have a geometric mean of one, although each sampled-token probability has changed tenfold. More generally, a response can appear well aligned under this score because its probability changes balance out, rather than because those changes are small.

We propose Cancellation-Aware Response Masking (CARM), a sequence-level mask that takes the absolute value of each token log-ratio before averaging. This prevents opposing probability changes from canceling while treating reciprocal changes symmetrically. Figure 1 illustrates the distinction on a real 8,619-token response: substantial positive and negative log-ratio contributions largely cancel under GeoMean, whereas CARM retains their magnitudes. CARM changes which responses contribute to optimization while retaining the token-level PPO/GRPO surrogate.

Beyond preventing cancellation, CARM gives the response-level threshold a direct token-level interpretation. We prove that every accepted response satisfies a joint bound on the fraction of sampled-token ratios outside a prescribed, possibly asymmetric band and their mean log-distance beyond its boundaries. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show improvements over token- and sequence-level baselines. Threshold analyses further show that similar filtering rates can yield different accuracies, while filtering more responses is not consistently better.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We formalize cancellation in signed-log sequence masking: the aggregate score can indicate perfect apparent alignment even when every sampled token ratio violates a prescribed band.

  • •

    We propose CARM, a sequence-level mask that prevents cancellation by taking absolute values before averaging token log-ratios. We derive a joint bound on the frequency and severity of ratio-band violations in accepted responses, including asymmetric bands, giving the filtering threshold a token-level interpretation.

  • •

    Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show improvements over sequence- and token-level baselines. Paired-response diagnostics and threshold analyses characterize the selection behavior: higher accuracy is observed at comparable average filtering rates, and accuracy is not monotone in the masked fraction.

2 Related Work

Policy optimization for LLM post-training. Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) constrains Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, while PPO uses a clipped-ratio surrogate (Schulman et al., 2015; Schulman et al., 2017). GRPO replaces a learned critic with within-group relative advantages (Shao et al., 2024). Answer correctness and program execution provide reward signals for improving mathematical reasoning and code generation (Le et al., 2022; Dou et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2026), complementing inference-time reasoning and program-aided prompting (Wei et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023). Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization (DAPO) refines clipping and sampling (Yu et al., 2025); related work revisits advantage normalization, sequence-level objectives, and reward–policy learning (Hu et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026a). These choices determine how sampled responses contribute to optimization. CARM addresses the complementary question of whether a sampled response should contribute to the current policy update.

Off-policy and token-level trust-region control. This selection problem arises even in nominally online training: actor–learner delay, repeated updates, and rollout–training engine differences separate the policy that generates responses from the policy being optimized (Espeholt et al., 2018; Yao et al., 2025; Sheng et al., 2025). Importance weighting and token-level filtering control individual update contributions (Espeholt et al., 2018; Shen et al., 2025). Adaptive clipping balances advantage contributions and mitigates entropy loss (Xi et al., 2026), while divergence-based controls constrain update size (Qi et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026). These mechanisms regulate the update within a response. CARM instead decides whether to retain the complete response, separating response selection from the surrogate applied to retained tokens.

Sequence-level correction and masking. Response-level selection must summarize mismatch across an entire sampled path. Length-normalized geometric aggregation removes the direct length dependence of multiplying token ratios (Liu et al., 2025b); it also underlies sequence-level clipping in Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) (Zheng et al., 2025a). DeepSeek-V3.2 explicitly uses off-policy sequence masking based on the mean signed log-ratio, equivalently the logarithm of a length-normalized geometric-mean ratio, to stabilize GRPO training (Liu et al., 2025a). Its rule applies a one-sided threshold to negative-advantage responses. Our GeoMean baseline uses the same signed-log aggregation with reciprocal-band acceptance (Eq. 5); we examine advantage conditioning separately in Section 5.2. TRM takes a worst-position view, rejecting a response when its maximum token-level divergence violates a long-horizon trust region (Li et al., 2026). CARM targets a different limitation: geometric aggregation averages signed log-ratios, so opposing shifts can cancel. Averaging their absolute values measures bidirectional drift rather than net displacement. The resulting mask changes which responses contribute to the update while retaining the token-level policy surrogate.

3 Method

3.1 Problem Setup

Let xx be a prompt and let yi=(yi,1,…,yi,Ti)y_{i}=(y_{i,1},\ldots,y_{i,T_{i}}) be the ii-th sampled response. We use response and sequence interchangeably for these generated tokens. We consider nonempty responses (Ti≥1T_{i}\geq 1) with finite token log-probabilities, so 0<ri,t<∞0<r_{i,t}<\infty. The token-level ratio of the current policy to the rollout policy is

ri,t​(θ)=πθ​(yi,t∣x,yi,<t)πrollout​(yi,t∣x,yi,<t).r_{i,t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\mathrm{rollout}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})}. (1)

For a sequence-level advantage A^i\hat{A}_{i}, the conventional asymmetric PPO/GRPO token surrogate is

ℓi,t​(θ)=min⁡(ri,t​(θ)​A^i,clip⁡(ri,t​(θ),1−ϵlow,1+ϵhigh)​A^i).\ell_{i,t}(\theta)=\min\Big(r_{i,t}(\theta)\hat{A}_{i},\operatorname{clip}\big(r_{i,t}(\theta),1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}\big)\hat{A}_{i}\Big). (2)

For a binary response mask Mi∈{0,1}M_{i}\in\{0,1\}, averaging the retained token losses gives

ℒmasked​(θ)=−∑iMi​∑t=1Tiℓi,t​(θ)∑iMi​Ti.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{masked}}(\theta)=-\frac{\sum_{i}M_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{i}}\ell_{i,t}(\theta)}{\sum_{i}M_{i}T_{i}}. (3)

The policy-loss contribution is defined as zero if no response is retained. CARM specifies the detached mask independently of loss normalization; Appendix B states the convention used in the experiments.

3.2 GeoMean Masking and Ratio Cancellation

Let G⁡(yi)=exp⁡(1Ti​∑tlog⁡ri,t)G(y_{i})=\exp(\frac{1}{T_{i}}\sum_{t}\log r_{i,t}) denote the geometric-mean token ratio. We define its log-space deviation and reciprocal-symmetric score as

dGeoMean​(yi)=|1Ti​∑t=1Tilog⁡ri,t|,sGeoMean​(yi)=exp⁡(dGeoMean​(yi)).d_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y_{i})=\left|\frac{1}{T_{i}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{i}}\log r_{i,t}\right|,\qquad s_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y_{i})=\exp(d_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y_{i})). (4)

The response is retained when

MiGeoMean=[sGeoMean(yi)≤τGeoMean].M_{i}^{\mathrm{GeoMean}}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[s_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y_{i})\leq\tau_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}\right]. (5)

For τGeoMean≥1\tau_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}\geq 1, this requires the geometric-mean ratio to lie in the reciprocal interval [1/τGeoMean,τGeoMean][1/\tau_{\mathrm{GeoMean}},\tau_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}]. Equivalently, dGeoMean=|log⁡G|d_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}=|\log G| and sGeoMean=max⁡(G,G−1)s_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}=\max(G,G^{-1}). We use GeoMean as a descriptive shorthand for this two-sided rule. It shares signed-log aggregation with DeepSeek-V3.2, whose mask instead uses a one-sided threshold on negative-advantage responses (Liu et al., 2025a).

Proposition 1 (Cancellation under signed aggregation).

For any B>1B>1 and any 1<c<B1<c<B, there exists an even-length response for which every token ratio lies outside [1/c,c][1/c,c], while sGeoMean​(y)=1s_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y)=1.

Proof.

Let the ratios alternate between BB and 1/B1/B. Every token is outside [1/c,c][1/c,c], but the log-ratios alternate between log⁡B\log B and −log⁡B-\log B. Their sum is zero, so dGeoMean​(y)=0d_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y)=0 and sGeoMean​(y)=1s_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y)=1. ∎

Proposition 1 does not claim that the exact trajectory likelihood ratio is incorrect. Indeed, πθ​(y∣x)/πrollout​(y∣x)=∏trt\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)/\pi_{\mathrm{rollout}}(y\mid x)=\prod_{t}r_{t}. It shows that thresholding a signed aggregate does not bound the magnitudes of the sampled-token log-ratios when used as a response-level filter. Figure 1 shows this cancellation in an actual unfiltered rollout.

3.3 Cancellation-Aware Response Masking

CARM removes direction before aggregation:

dCARM​(yi)=1Ti​∑t=1Ti|log⁡ri,t|,sCARM​(yi)=exp⁡(dCARM​(yi)).d_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y_{i})=\frac{1}{T_{i}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{i}}\left|\log r_{i,t}\right|,\qquad s_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y_{i})=\exp(d_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y_{i})). (6)

Equivalently, each token contributes the reciprocal-invariant mismatch max⁡(ri,t,ri,t−1)\max(r_{i,t},r_{i,t}^{-1}) in ratio space, since |log⁡(1/ri,t)|=|log⁡ri,t||\log(1/r_{i,t})|=|\log r_{i,t}|. The CARM mask is

MiCARM=[sCARM(yi)≤τCARM].M_{i}^{\mathrm{CARM}}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[s_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y_{i})\leq\tau_{\mathrm{CARM}}\right]. (7)

During optimization, the response mask and token-level surrogate use the same current-policy forward pass and the stored rollout log-probabilities, before the optimizer update. The binary gate is treated as a constant during backpropagation; a rejected response contributes no policy-loss gradient in that update. Algorithm 1 and Appendix B give the computation schedule and numerical conventions.

The two scores measure different properties: GeoMean measures the magnitude of the average signed log-ratio, whereas CARM measures the average log-ratio magnitude. Mean-absolute aggregation combines contributions linearly, preventing cancellation without selecting only the most extreme token or squaring each deviation. Figure 2 contrasts this rule with GeoMean.

A real disagreement case from an unfiltered rollout.

We replay both masks on an unfiltered batch of 1,024 responses generated by Qwen3.5-4B. With τGeoMean=1.005\tau_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}=1.005 and τCARM=1.02\tau_{\mathrm{CARM}}=1.02, 160 responses are accepted by both rules, 668 are rejected by both, 195 are accepted only by GeoMean, and one is accepted only by CARM. Figure 1 visualizes a representative GeoMean-only response whose opposing log-ratio masses cancel; Appendix C provides all 8,619 tokens. Its mean absolute log-ratio is 9.799.79 times the absolute signed mean, while the largest single-token contribution accounts for only 0.43%0.43\% of the absolute log-ratio mass. The discrepancy is therefore not driven by one extreme token. These unequal thresholds illustrate different filtering decisions; the shared-threshold relation is examined separately below.

Proposition 2 (Acceptance-set inclusion).

For every response yy, sCARM​(y)≥sGeoMean​(y)s_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y)\geq s_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y). Thus, for any shared threshold τ≥1\tau\geq 1,

{y:sCARM​(y)≤τ}⊆{y:sGeoMean​(y)≤τ}.\{y:s_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y)\leq\tau\}\subseteq\{y:s_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y)\leq\tau\}. (8)
Proof.

The triangle inequality gives

1T​∑t|log⁡rt|≥|1T​∑tlog⁡rt|.\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}|\log r_{t}|\geq\left|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\log r_{t}\right|.

Exponentiation preserves the inequality, and the accepted-set inclusion follows immediately. ∎

Figure 3 replays both statistics on the same 1,024 responses from an unfiltered rollout batch, before any sequence-level gate can alter the training trajectory. Every response obeys dCARM≥dGeoMeand_{\mathrm{CARM}}\geq d_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}, with no numerical violations; the mean difference is 0.03190.0319. At every shared threshold, CARM rejects at least as many responses as GeoMean, in agreement with Proposition 2.

𝒱−\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{-} ={t:rt<ℓ},\displaystyle=\{t:r_{t}<\ell\}, p−\displaystyle p_{-} =|𝒱−|T,\displaystyle=\frac{|\mathcal{V}_{-}|}{T}, (9)

Let pout=p−+p+p_{\mathrm{out}}=p_{-}+p_{+} and define the log-costs of reaching the boundaries by b−=log⁡(1/ℓ)b_{-}=\log(1/\ell) and b+=log⁡ub_{+}=\log u. For pout>0p_{\mathrm{out}}>0, define

and set δ¯out​(y)=0\bar{\delta}_{\mathrm{out}}(y)=0 when pout=0p_{\mathrm{out}}=0. We call δ¯out\bar{\delta}_{\mathrm{out}} the mean violation severity: it is the average log-distance by which an out-of-band token passes its nearest boundary.

Proposition 3 (Bounds on ratio-band violations).

If sCARM​(y)≤τs_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y)\leq\tau with τ≥1\tau\geq 1, then

p−​b−+p+​b++pout​δ¯out​(y)≤log⁡τ.p_{-}b_{-}+p_{+}b_{+}+p_{\mathrm{out}}\bar{\delta}_{\mathrm{out}}(y)\leq\log\tau. (12)

Consequently, with bmin=min⁡(b−,b+)b_{\min}=\min(b_{-},b_{+}),

pout≤min⁡{1,log⁡τbmin+δ¯out​(y)}≤min⁡{1,log⁡τbmin}.p_{\mathrm{out}}\leq\min\!\left\{1,\frac{\log\tau}{b_{\min}+\bar{\delta}_{\mathrm{out}}(y)}\right\}\leq\min\!\left\{1,\frac{\log\tau}{b_{\min}}\right\}. (13)

At a fixed threshold, more severe violations imply a smaller admissible fraction; the bound does not require a reciprocal-symmetric band. This is a deterministic bound on the sampled-token ratios, not on the full conditional-policy KL divergence.

Proof.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Experiments use verl (Sheng et al., 2025) and GRPO. We train Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) on DAPO Math (Yu et al., 2025) and evaluate AIME 2024/2025/2026 (Mathematical Association of America, 2026) and BeyondAIME (Chen et al., 2025) with 16 responses per problem. For code generation, Qwen3.5-9B is trained on the TACO training split (Li et al., 2023) with executable rewards. Evaluation uses the held-out TACO test split, LiveCodeBench-v6 (Jain et al., 2025), and the EvalPlus suites HumanEval+ and MBPP+ (Liu et al., 2023). Metrics are obtained using three random seeds for both tasks. Math-Verify checks mathematical answers (Kydlíček, 2025); SandboxFusion executes and judges generated code (Cheng et al., 2025). Baselines are Null, IcePop, TRM, and GeoMean. Null retains the same GRPO procedure, including token-level clipping and advantage normalization, but applies no additional off-policy response mask. Appendix D and Table 3 give the datasets, prompts, and configuration.

4.2 Mathematical Reasoning

Table 1 compares mathematical reasoning across AIME 2024/2025/2026 and BeyondAIME. CARM achieves the highest four-dataset average for both Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B. Its three-year AIME average also exceeds those of Null, IcePop, TRM, and GeoMean: relative to GeoMean, it rises from 69.17%69.17\% to 70.42%70.42\% on Qwen3.5-4B and from 74.03%74.03\% to 77.50%77.50\% on Qwen3.5-9B. The latter improvement holds separately on all three AIME years. For Qwen3.5-4B, CARM improves AIME 2024, ties on AIME 2025, and is slightly lower on AIME 2026, while improving the aggregate.

On BeyondAIME, CARM raises mean@16 from 38.88%38.88\% to 42.56%42.56\% on Qwen3.5-4B and from 47.06%47.06\% to 49.19%49.19\% on Qwen3.5-9B relative to GeoMean. The gains therefore extend beyond the annual AIME benchmarks. Across all four datasets, the Average increases from 61.59%61.59\% to 63.45%63.45\% on Qwen3.5-4B and from 67.29%67.29\% to 70.42%70.42\% on Qwen3.5-9B. For the larger model, the aggregate lead accompanies an improvement on every benchmark; for the smaller model, it reflects an overall gain with a mixed year-by-year AIME pattern.

Relative to TRM, CARM improves the three-year AIME average by 8.138.13 points on Qwen3.5-4B and 3.543.54 points on Qwen3.5-9B despite TRM’s higher rejection rates (Section 5.1). Relative to IcePop, CARM improves the four-dataset Average by 26.5426.54 points on Qwen3.5-4B and 12.5212.52 points on Qwen3.5-9B.

4.3 Code Generation

Table 2 reports pass@1 for Qwen3.5-9B trained on the TACO training split. Testing on TACO measures performance on held-out problems from the same dataset, while LiveCodeBench-v6, HumanEval+, and MBPP+ evaluate the resulting policy on three additional benchmarks.

CARM improves average pass@1 by 3.033.03 points over GeoMean and 2.882.88 points over IcePop, the strongest baseline on average. The gains are not uniform: relative to GeoMean, the increase is modest on TACO, from 46.03%46.03\% to 46.70%46.70\%, and largest on LiveCodeBench-v6, from 44.50%44.50\% to 51.20%51.20\%. On HumanEval+ and MBPP+, CARM reaches 94.11%94.11\% and 81.22%81.22\%, also exceeding IcePop, the strongest baseline on these suites. Thus, the improvement is not confined to held-out TACO problems.

5 Analysis

We examine whether the gains are explained by filtering more responses, whether advantage sign should override the gate, and whether improvements persist across different sampling criteria.

5.1 Update Redundancy and Effective Filtering

We use update redundancy to describe improved validation accuracy despite omitting response-level updates, without implying that rejected responses lack useful information.

GeoMean and CARM mask an average of 55.65%55.65\% and 54.52%54.52\% of sequences during Qwen3.5-4B training, yet improve three-year AIME mean@16 over Null by 18.3318.33 and 19.5819.58 points. For Qwen3.5-9B, the corresponding fractions are 52.75%52.75\% and 52.32%52.32\%, with gains of 3.613.61 and 7.087.08 points. Filtering persists throughout training (Appendix Figure 9). Filtering already-generated responses complements selective rollout use and data-efficient reasoning (Yu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025b).

Figure 4 compares AIME accuracy with mean sequence-masked fraction. On Qwen3.5-9B, CARM outperforms GeoMean by 3.473.47 points while their masked fractions differ by only 0.430.43 points. Accuracy is not monotone in the masked fraction, and TRM rejects more responses without outperforming CARM.

Paired-score differences (Figure 3) show that rejection rates alone do not characterize retained trajectories. Tightening CARM’s frequency–severity budget (Proposition 3) limits sampled-token mismatch but removes update contributions, consistent with the observed non-monotonicity.

5.2 Advantage-Conditional Masking Ablation

DeepSeek-V3.2 masks only negative-advantage responses (Liu et al., 2025a). We test this conditioning on Qwen3.5-9B with CARM’s score and threshold fixed within each task. Standard masking reaches 75.63%75.63\% AIME mean@16 (2024/2025/2026) versus 60.28%60.28\% for negative-only masking; LiveCodeBench-v6 scores are 50.58%50.58\% versus 42.22%42.22\% (Figure 6).

Even a correctly rewarded response can be stale if the current policy assigns substantially different probabilities to its tokens. PPO clips positive-advantage terms above the upper ratio bound, but other token updates can remain active (Schulman et al., 2017); it does not enforce a response-level trust region (Li et al., 2026). These results suggest that response-level mismatch checks can remain useful even for positive-advantage responses.

5.3 Sampling Consistency

We assess sampling consistency using bootstrapped best-of-kk and worst-of-kk: the former requires at least one correct response among kk, while the latter requires all kk to be correct. Worst-of-kk measures sampling repeatability, not distribution-shift or adversarial robustness. Appendix G defines the estimators and reports results for k∈{1,2,4,8,16}k\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}.

For Qwen3.5-9B, Figure 6 averages results over AIME 2024/2025/2026. CARM improves mean@16, best@16, and worst@16 over GeoMean by 3.473.47, 2.742.74, and 2.782.78 points, respectively; the corresponding gains over TRM are 3.543.54, 0.300.30, and 4.614.61 points. CARM also achieves the highest best-of-kk and worst-of-kk values throughout the displayed range.

6 Conclusion

We proposed CARM, a response-level off-policy mask that averages absolute token log-ratios to prevent opposing probability changes from canceling. Our analysis shows that signed aggregation can accept responses even when every sampled-token ratio lies outside a reciprocal-symmetric band. In contrast, CARMbounds the frequency and severity of ratio-band violations through a joint budget for each accepted response, giving the threshold a token-level interpretation. Experiments show gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation over the evaluated baselines, together with improved sampling consistency. These findings support CARM as a principled response-selection criterion that complements reward-directed PPO/GRPO optimization.

Appendix A Detailed Proofs

A.1 Proof of Proposition 1

Step 1: construct an even-length response.

Fix arbitrary constants B>1B>1 and 1<c<B1<c<B. Choose an arbitrary positive integer mm and let the response length be T=2​mT=2m. For every pair j∈{1,…,m}j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}, define

r2​j−1=B,r2​j=1B.r_{2j-1}=B,\qquad r_{2j}=\frac{1}{B}. (15)

Thus the response contains exactly mm ratios equal to BB and exactly mm ratios equal to 1/B1/B. These ratios can arise from valid conditional policies: at each odd position, assign the sampled token probabilities 1/(1+B)1/(1+B) under the rollout policy and B/(1+B)B/(1+B) under the current policy, and swap them at each even position. Assign the remaining probability to a second token. Both policies are normalized, all probabilities are positive, and their sampled-token ratios are exactly those in Equation 15.

Step 2: verify that every ratio violates the band.

For each odd position, r2​j−1=B>cr_{2j-1}=B>c, so it lies strictly above the upper endpoint of [1/c,c][1/c,c]. For each even position, 1<c<B1<c<B and all quantities are positive. Taking reciprocals reverses the inequalities and gives

1>1c>1B.1>\frac{1}{c}>\frac{1}{B}. (16)

Hence r2​j=1/B<1/cr_{2j}=1/B<1/c, so it lies strictly below the lower endpoint. Therefore every one of the TT token ratios is outside [1/c,c][1/c,c].

Step 3: evaluate the GeoMean statistic.

The logarithm of a reciprocal satisfies log⁡(1/B)=−log⁡B\log(1/B)=-\log B. Grouping the signed log-ratios into the mm adjacent pairs in Equation 15 yields

∑t=1Tlog⁡rt\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log r_{t} =∑j=1m(log⁡B+log⁡(1/B))\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(\log B+\log(1/B)\right) (17)
=∑j=1m(log⁡B−log⁡B)\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(\log B-\log B\right) (18)
=∑j=1m0\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}0 (19)
=0.\displaystyle=0. (20)

Substitution into Equation 4 gives

dGeoMean​(y)\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y) =|1T​∑t=1Tlog⁡rt|\displaystyle=\left|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log r_{t}\right| (21)
=|0T|\displaystyle=\left|\frac{0}{T}\right| (22)
=0,\displaystyle=0, (23)

and therefore

sGeoMean​(y)=exp⁡(dGeoMean​(y))=exp⁡(0)=1.s_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y)=\exp(d_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y))=\exp(0)=1. (24)

This proves the proposition: every token can violate the prescribed reciprocal band even though GeoMean reports its minimum possible score.

Step 4: evaluate the CARM statistic for comparison.

Because B>1B>1, log⁡B>0\log B>0, and hence |log⁡B|=|log⁡(1/B)|=log⁡B|\log B|=|\log(1/B)|=\log B. Consequently,

dCARM​(y)\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y) =1T​∑t=1T|log⁡rt|\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}|\log r_{t}| (25)
=12​m​∑j=1m(|log⁡B|+|log⁡(1/B)|)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(|\log B|+|\log(1/B)|\right) (26)
=12​m​∑j=1m2​log⁡B\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}2\log B (27)
=log⁡B,\displaystyle=\log B, (28)

so sCARM​(y)=exp⁡(log⁡B)=Bs_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y)=\exp(\log B)=B. Thus any GeoMean threshold at least one accepts this construction, whereas CARM rejects it whenever τCARM<B\tau_{\mathrm{CARM}}<B.

A.2 Proof of Proposition 2

Step 1: move to log-ratio coordinates.

For a fixed response of positive length TT, set zt=log⁡rt∈ℝz_{t}=\log r_{t}\in\mathbb{R}. For T=1T=1, both scores are identical. For T≥2T\geq 2, the triangle inequality applied repeatedly to the finite sum gives

|∑t=1Tzt|\displaystyle\left|\sum_{t=1}^{T}z_{t}\right| =|z1+(z2+⋯+zT)|\displaystyle=|z_{1}+(z_{2}+\cdots+z_{T})| (29)
≤|z1|+|z2+⋯+zT|\displaystyle\leq|z_{1}|+|z_{2}+\cdots+z_{T}| (30)
≤⋯≤∑t=1T|zt|.\displaystyle\leq\cdots\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}|z_{t}|. (31)

Step 2: normalize by response length.

Since T>0T>0, division by TT preserves the direction of the inequality:

|1T​∑tzt|≤1T​∑t|zt|.\left|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}z_{t}\right|\leq\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}|z_{t}|. (32)

Using zt=log⁡rtz_{t}=\log r_{t} and Equations 4 and 6, the left-hand side is exactly dGeoMean​(y)d_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y) and the right-hand side is exactly dCARM​(y)d_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y). Therefore

dGeoMean​(y)≤dCARM​(y).d_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y)\leq d_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y). (33)

The exponential function is strictly increasing on ℝ\mathbb{R}. Applying it to both sides gives

exp⁡(dGeoMean​(y))\displaystyle\exp(d_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y)) ≤exp⁡(dCARM​(y)),\displaystyle\leq\exp(d_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y)), (34)

This proves the pointwise score inequality.

Step 4: prove accepted-set inclusion.

Take an arbitrary response y∈{y:sCARM​(y)≤τ}y\in\{y:s_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y)\leq\tau\}. By membership in this set, sCARM​(y)≤τs_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y)\leq\tau. Combining this fact with the pointwise result from Step 3 gives

sGeoMean​(y)≤sCARM​(y)≤τ.s_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y)\leq s_{\mathrm{CARM}}(y)\leq\tau. (36)

Thus y∈{y:sGeoMean​(y)≤τ}y\in\{y:s_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}(y)\leq\tau\}. Since the argument holds for every element of the CARM accepted set, Equation 8 follows.

Equality condition.

For real scalars, equality in the triangle inequality holds exactly when all nonzero ztz_{t} have the same sign. Accordingly, sGeoMean=sCARMs_{\mathrm{GeoMean}}=s_{\mathrm{CARM}} when all nonzero token log-ratios are nonnegative or all are nonpositive. If at least one zt>0z_{t}>0 and at least one zt′<0z_{t^{\prime}}<0, the inequality is strict.

Appendix B Implementation of CARM

Algorithm 1 gives the response-level masking rule, treating the hard threshold decision as constant during backpropagation. The gate changes which response losses contribute to an update while retaining the token-level PPO/GRPO surrogate.

Mask computation schedule.

We store the sampled-token log-probabilities produced during rollout. During training, each optimizer mini-batch is divided into micro-batches; each micro-batch forward supplies the current log-probabilities used by both the response mask and the token surrogate. The optimizer updates the policy after gradient accumulation over the mini-batch. Threshold comparisons produce a binary gate with no gradient through the decision, as represented by stopgrad\operatorname{stopgrad} in Algorithm 1. Masking is local to loss evaluation rather than permanent removal from the rollout batch. Our experiments use one optimization epoch per rollout batch; with multiple epochs, the gate would be recomputed whenever a response is evaluated under the updated policy.

The PPO/GRPO loss implementation in verl also applies dual clipping to negative advantages. Writing ℓi,t\ell_{i,t} for Equation 2, its surrogate is

ℓi,tdual={max⁡{ℓi,t,cdual​A^i},A^i<0,ℓi,t,A^i≥0,cdual=3.\ell^{\mathrm{dual}}_{i,t}=\begin{cases}\max\{\ell_{i,t},c_{\mathrm{dual}}\hat{A}_{i}\},&\hat{A}_{i}<0,\\ \ell_{i,t},&\hat{A}_{i}\geq 0,\end{cases}\qquad c_{\mathrm{dual}}=3. (72)

The sequence mask multiplies this surrogate without changing its clipping rule or normalization.

Numerical convention.

The theoretical scores use exact log-ratios. The implementation uses verl’s numerical guard z~t=clip⁡(log⁡rt,−20,20)\widetilde{z}_{t}=\operatorname{clip}(\log r_{t},-20,20) when computing the mask and token surrogate. If the guard is inactive, the implemented and theoretical scores coincide. Otherwise, the score inequalities and frequency–severity budget apply to the effective ratios r~t=exp⁡(z~t)\widetilde{r}_{t}=\exp(\widetilde{z}_{t}). For a band strictly inside [e−20,e20][e^{-20},e^{20}], including [0.8,1.28][0.8,1.28], clipping does not change which tokens violate the band. Thus the frequency-only guarantee also holds for the original ratios, while the severity term measures the guarded log-distances.

Appendix D Experimental Settings

D.1 Data

Math training data.

The mathematical-reasoning experiments use the competition-style problems in the DAPO Math training corpus (Yu et al., 2025). Math-Verify (Kydlíček, 2025) extracts the boxed final answer and checks its equivalence to the reference. Null, IcePop, TRM, GeoMean, and CARM use the same prompt order, rollout group size, rewards, optimizer settings, and token-level PPO/GRPO clipping; only the off-policy correction differs.

Math evaluation data.

AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and AIME 2026 each contain 30 contest problems and are reported separately (Mathematical Association of America, 2026). BeyondAIME contributes 100 additional problems designed to extend evaluation beyond the three annual AIME sets (Chen et al., 2025). We sample 16 responses per problem and compute acc/mean@16 from exact final-answer correctness. The Average in Table 1 gives AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AIME 2026, and BeyondAIME equal weight. Evaluation is performed before training and periodically during optimization.

Code training data.

The general-code experiments use problems from the TACO training split (Li et al., 2023), with natural-language task descriptions, input/output specifications, and executable tests. During RL, the reward checks up to the first ten available tests for each training problem. This fixed cap keeps execution cost and sandbox load comparable across methods; held-out benchmark tests are not used by the training reward. All five methods receive the same prompts, decoding budget, executable reward, and optimizer configuration.

Code evaluation data.

We evaluate each frozen TACO-trained checkpoint on four complementary suites. TACO evaluation uses 1,000 problems from its held-out test split and up to the first ten tests per problem. LiveCodeBench-v6 contains 1,054 temporally collected coding problems and is judged with its complete released tests. HumanEval+ and MBPP+ contain 164 and 378 problems, respectively, and use the stronger EvalPlus test suites rather than only the original base tests. MBPP+ extends the MBPP benchmark (Austin et al., 2021). Every generated program is rejudged with SandboxFusion (Cheng et al., 2025), with functional correctness reported as pass@1.

D.2 Prompt Templates

Figures 7 and 8 reproduce the task-specific chat messages used throughout training and evaluation. Dataset problem statements replace the placeholders without changing the surrounding instructions.

D.3 Training and Evaluation Configuration

Table 3 consolidates the shared settings, method-specific controls, and threshold grids used to produce the reported comparisons.

Evaluation protocol.

Both tasks are evaluated with three random seeds. Mathematical-reasoning evaluation uses 16 responses per problem and reports mean@16; code-generation evaluation uses one response per problem and reports pass@1. Code decoding uses temperature 0.70.7, top-p=0.9p=0.9, top-k=50k=50, and a maximum response length of 16,384 tokens. Generated programs are judged with the same batched SandboxFusion evaluator across methods.

For each method, math results use the training iterate with the highest three-year AIME mean@16; code results use the iterate with the highest LiveCodeBench-v6 validation pass@1. Best- and worst-of-kk use the same math iterate without separate optimization of either metric. Qwen3.5-4B BeyondAIME results for Null, GeoMean, and CARM use separate runs matched in configuration and training iteration.

TRM implementation.

We follow the sampled-token max-filtering option described in Section 4.3 and Appendix E of Li et al. (2026). It rejects a response when maxt⁡12​(log⁡rt)2>0.05\max_{t}\frac{1}{2}(\log r_{t})^{2}>0.05. This is the paper’s proposed approximation when full logits are unavailable, not a full-vocabulary KL implementation. All TRM results in this paper refer to this sampled-token variant.

Appendix G Best- and Worst-of-kk Sampling Metrics

Figure 6 evaluates inference-time sample scaling at the same Qwen3.5-9B checkpoints reported in Table 5. For each problem, let X1,…,X16∈{0,1}X_{1},\ldots,X_{16}\in\{0,1\} denote the correctness of the 16 independently sampled responses and let c=∑j=116Xjc=\sum_{j=1}^{16}X_{j}. The per-problem empirical accuracy is c/16c/16, and mean@16 averages this quantity over problems and then equally over AIME 2024, 2025, and 2026.

Best-of-kk asks whether at least one of kk sampled responses is correct. It captures the opportunity provided by additional inference-time sampling when an oracle verifier can select a correct candidate. Worst-of-kk asks whether all kk sampled responses are correct. It is therefore a strict measure of repeatability: a model scores highly only when its stochastic samples solve the same problem consistently. Worst-of-kk should not be read as robustness to distribution shift or adversarial perturbations. At k=1k=1, both statistics reduce exactly to mean@16, which anchors the two curves at the same observed single-sample accuracy.

For k∈{2,4,8,16}k\in\{2,4,8,16\}, we resample kk responses with replacement from the 16 available responses for each problem and apply the maximum (best-of-kk) or minimum (worst-of-kk) correctness operator. The plotted values average 1,000 bootstrap replicates, using the same models as Table 1.

For a problem with cc correct responses among 16, the expected best-of-kk value is

B^k​(c)=1−(1−c16)k.\widehat{B}_{k}(c)=1-\left(1-\frac{c}{16}\right)^{k}. (73)

Equation 73 is the probability that at least one of kk independent draws from the empirical response distribution is correct. It is a with-replacement best-of-kk statistic, not the standard without-replacement pass@kk estimator. The corresponding expected worst-of-kk value is

W^k​(c)=(c16)k.\widehat{W}_{k}(c)=\left(\frac{c}{16}\right)^{k}. (74)

Equation 74 is the probability that all kk draws are correct. It is non-increasing in kk, and strictly decreasing for a problem when 0<c<160<c<16. As with best-of-kk, this is a with-replacement statistic rather than the literal maximum or minimum over a fixed subset of the original 16 responses. Together, the two curves characterize solution coverage and repeatability. Worst-of-kk emphasizes problems with high per-problem correctness probability; an aggregate increase does not imply improvement on every problem.
